title: Arrays
summary: An array is an ordered list of values. You can use one to store names, scores or things in a bag.
introduction: An array is an ordered list of values. You can use one to store names, scores or things in a bag. Make a short list. Find an item by its position, add a new item and work through the list one item at a time.
learningObjectives: Create arrays, read elements by index and change their length
Add, remove and find elements with the built-in methods
Transform arrays with map, filter and reduce instead of loops
Tell mutating methods from the ones that return a new array

blocks.text: An array literal is a comma-separated list in square brackets. Positions, called **indexes**, start at `0`, so the last element is at `length - 1`; the newer `at()` method accepts negative positions counted from the end. Reading a position that does not exist gives `undefined` rather than an error.

blocks.text: `join(", ")` turns the array into one string with a separator between elements. The examples use it to print arrays on a single line; in the browser's developer tools you can also log the array itself and expand it.

`push` and `pop` work at the end of the array; `unshift` and `shift` work at the start. All four change the array in place (they **mutate** it), and `pop` and `shift` return the element they removed. Because inserting at the start moves every other element, `push`/`pop` are the fast pair.

blocks.text: `includes` answers 'is this value in the array?' and `indexOf` tells you where (or `-1` if absent). For anything more complex than equality, `find` and `findIndex` take a function that tests each element and stop at the first match. `some` and `every` return a boolean for 'at least one' and 'all'.

These three methods express the most common loops as single, readable calls, and none of them changes the original array. `map` builds a new array by applying a function to every element. `filter` keeps only the elements for which the function returns true. `reduce` boils the array down to one value: it calls your function with an accumulator and each element, and the second argument is the accumulator's starting value.

Because each method returns an array, they chain. The example below turns a list of task objects into the titles of the unfinished ones, and uses `forEach` for the one case where you only want a side effect per element, such as printing.

blocks.text: `sort` compares elements as strings unless you give it a compare function, which is why `[10, 9, 1]` sorts as `1, 10, 9`. For numbers pass `(a, b) => a - b`. `sort` and `reverse` mutate the array; the newer `toSorted` and `toReversed` (ES2023, supported in all current browsers) return a sorted copy and leave the original alone. `slice(start, end)` copies a range without the end index; `splice` removes or inserts elements in place.

blocks.title: sort() without a compare function
blocks.text: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]` because every element is converted to a string and `"10"` comes before `"9"`. Always pass a compare function for numbers: `(a, b) => a - b` ascending, `(a, b) => b - a` descending. Remember too that `sort` reorders the original array; use `toSorted` when you still need the old order.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Start from `const words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]`. Produce the lengths of each word with `map`, keep the words longer than three letters with `filter`, and compute the total number of letters with `reduce`. Then sort the words by length using `toSorted` with a compare function.

questions.question: Which method removes the last element of an array and returns it?
questions.explanation: pop removes from the end and returns the element; shift does the same at the start. slice copies and does not remove anything.

questions.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].filter((n) => n > 1).length` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: filter keeps the elements for which the function returns true: 2 and 3. The resulting array has two elements.
